summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Legal sufficiency review of a termination finding asks whether a reasonable factfinder could have formed a firm belief or conviction that the ground was proved, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the finding.
key_cases.relevance: Where the evidence fails this standard, rendition in the parent's favor — return of the child — is generally required.
key_cases.quote: look at all the evidence in the light most favorable to the finding to determine whether a reasonable trier of fact could have formed a firm belief

key_cases.case_name: In re Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The mass removal of children from the YFZ Ranch was not warranted on the evidence, because Chapter 262 requires danger to the individual child and the Family Code gives courts ample authority to protect children without separating them from their parents.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas Supreme Court's controlling application of Family Code §§ 262.101-.201 at this node: danger must be proved as to the particular child, and the court must use the Code's lesser alternatives — orders restraining a party, removing the alleged perpetrator, or assisting the investigation — before separating a family.
key_cases.quote: the Family Code gives the district court broad authority to protect children short of separating them from their parents and placing them in foster care

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Title IV-E's 'reasonable efforts' requirement creates no federal right enforceable by children or parents under 42 U.S.C. § 1983; enforcement runs through HHS and the state-plan process.
key_cases.relevance: Determines the enforcement channel for the federal requirement behind this node: the Title IV-E/ASFA command is not privately enforceable, so compliance is policed by HHS, the state plan and the CFSR — not by a parent's or child's lawsuit.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

notice_requirements.timing: Citation on the filing of an original petition shall be issued and served as in other civil cases (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(c)); citation by publication, available only for persons entitled to service who cannot be notified by personal service or registered or certified mail and for persons whose names are unknown, must be published not later than the 20th day before the date set for the hearing (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.010(a)-(b))
content_required: Service of citation on the filing of a petition in an original suit is required for each parent as to whom the parent-child relationship has not been terminated or process has not been waived under Chapter 161, an alleged father unless an affidavit of waiver of interest is attached or the petitioner has complied with § 161.002(b)(2), (3), or (4), a man who has filed a notice of intent to claim paternity, a managing or possessory conservator, a person having possession of or access to the child under an order, a guardian of the person or estate of the child, and the Department of Family and Protective Services if the petition requests that it be appointed managing conservator (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(a))
Citation may be served on any other person who has or who may assert an interest in the child (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.009(b))

Citation by publication must state that the respondent has been sued, that the respondent may employ an attorney, that a default judgment may be taken unless a written answer is filed with the clerk who issued the citation by 10 a.m. on the Monday next following the expiration of 20 days after service, and the style, number, court, and filing date of the suit (Tex. Fam. Code § 102.010(c))

Immediately after a court renders an order terminating the parent-child relationship in a suit filed by the department, the department must notify each individual identified under § 262.1095 and described by § 102.006(c) that the parent-child relationship has been terminated and that the individual has 90 days after the date the order is rendered to file a suit requesting managing conservatorship (Tex. Fam. Code § 161.2081)
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Notwithstanding Rule 329, Texas Rules of Civil Procedure, the validity of an order terminating the parental rights of a person who has been personally served, who executed an affidavit of relinquishment or waiver of interest, or whose rights were terminated under § 161.002(b) — and of an order terminating the rights of a person served by citation by publication — is not subject to collateral or direct attack after the sixth month after the date the order was signed (Tex. Fam. Code § 161.211(a)-(b))
